In this blog, we'll highlight: * What is lab procurement? * Why is efficient lab procurement essential? * Common challenges in lab procurement * Value of inventory management systems for lab procurement * Top tips for optimizing lab procurement ## **What is lab procurement?** Lab procurement encompasses the activities involved in ordering, purchasing, and replenishing inventory within a laboratory setting. This includes sourcing high-quality materials and specialized equipment, managing relationships with a diverse array of vendors, and ensuring that the lab is always stocked with the necessary supplies to maintain uninterrupted operations and facilitate ground-breaking research. Get it right and researchers have what they need when they need it. Get it wrong and you're looking at delayed experiments, budget overruns, and materials that arrive without the safety documentation your compliance team needs. Procurement is also where [**inventory management**](https://www.scisure.com/uses/inventory-management)begins. Every order eventually becomes a container on a shelf that someone has to find, use, and dispose of. [![Inventory management with SciSure LIMS](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/67f67c38815f9f85e958075a/6a465716bc5af1a0897956e7_Inventory%20management%20SciSure%20LIMS.png)](https://www.scisure.com/lims) Inventory management with SciSure LIMS ## **Why is efficient lab procurement essential?** Efficient lab procurement is fundamental to the success and sustainability of laboratory operations. Here's why: ### **Operational efficiency** Efficient procurement processes are crucial for maintaining operational continuity. For example, a research lab that uses a streamlined procurement system can quickly reorder essential reagents before they run out, ensuring that experiments are not delayed due to missing supplies. ### **Cost management** Effective procurement processes help laboratories manage costs more efficiently. This enables the lab to allocate resources to other critical areas, such as new research initiatives or advanced equipment purchases. ### **Compliance and quality** Maintaining high standards of quality and compliance is non-negotiable in laboratory settings. Effective procurement ensures that only certified, high-quality materials are purchased, supporting the lab's commitment to excellence. ### **Time savings** Streamlined procurement processes reduce the time spent on sourcing and purchasing materials. For example, using an automated procurement system that integrates with inventory management software can significantly cut down the time lab staff spend on administrative tasks. This allows them to focus more on their research, leading to increased productivity and faster project completion. ### **Supplier relationships** Developing strong relationships with reliable suppliers through efficient procurement practices can lead to better pricing, prioritized service, and access to exclusive products. For instance, a lab that has a long-term partnership with a chemical supplier might receive priority shipping and bulk discounts. ### Supply chain resilience Supply volatility has gone from occasional to constant. Lab Manager reports that [2025 US tariffs on imported plastics, reagents, PPE, and instrument components](https://www.labmanager.com/building-a-resilient-laboratory-supply-chain-in-an-era-of-disruption-35048) have pushed procurement costs up and changed cost-per-test calculations for labs working to fixed budgets. Deloitte's global survey of biopharma and medtech executives found [39% naming geopolitical tension as a top concern, with 38% pointing to inflation and supply chain risk](https://www.pharmamanufacturing.com/quality-risk/supply-chain/article/55337737/manufacturing-supply-chain-risks-in-2026-will-continue-to-weigh-on-life-sciences). Labs that map where they're exposed, keep a second qualified supplier for critical items, and know their real consumption rates absorb these shocks better than labs that reorder out of habit. Navigating these obstacles is crucial to ensure the smooth operation of lab activities and sustained progress in research and diagnostics: ### **Manual processes** Traditional procurement methods often rely on manual processes, which can be time-consuming and prone to errors. Manually tracking inventory and placing orders can lead to inaccuracies and inefficiencies. These manual tasks also consume significant labor resources, diverting staff from more critical and value-adding activities. The added risk of human error can result in delays and mismanagement, ultimately affecting the lab's productivity and service quality. ### **Lack of real-time data** Most labs can tell you what they ordered, but far fewer can tell you where it is, what condition it's in, or when it expires. That gap is where the money goes: duplicate orders because nobody could find the first one, reagents that expire in a fridge, and disposal fees on bulk purchases that looked like savings on the quote. It also eats time. ZAGENO's survey put the average at [six hours a week per lab professional just chasing order status](https://go.zageno.com/blog/stop-the-wild-goose-chase-how-to-spend-less-time-tracking-lab-supply-orders), rising to around 22 hours for procurement staff. ### **Vendor management** Managing relationships with multiple vendors and ensuring timely delivery of materials can be complex and demanding. Labs must coordinate with various suppliers to meet their diverse needs, ranging from scientific reagents to specialized equipment. This requires meticulous planning and organization to prevent delays and ensure that the quality and specifications of the materials meet the lab's standards. Effective vendor management also involves negotiating favorable terms and maintaining good relationships to secure reliable supply chains. ### Disconnected systems Ordering happens in one system, inventory in another, and chemical safety records in a third. Every handoff between them is a manual transcription step, and every manual step is a place where data goes stale. Learn more on our guide to [how fragmented lab systems increase organizational risk](https://www.scisure.com/blog/5-ways-fragmented-lab-systems-increase-organizational-risk). ### **Cost control** Effective cost control is essential in lab procurement. Balancing budgets while ensuring that all necessary supplies are available requires careful planning and monitoring. Labs must implement strategies to minimize costs without compromising on quality, which involves constant evaluation of procurement practices, seeking competitive pricing, and leveraging bulk purchasing where feasible. Ongoing cost analysis and budget adjustments are necessary to maintain financial health while supporting the lab's operational needs and goals. ## **The value of inventory management systems for lab procurement** Digital inventory systems close the gap between what was ordered and what's actually on the shelf. Supply chain management is the wider view, covering where your materials originate, how many suppliers you depend on for a given item, lead times, and what happens if one of them fails. A lab can have tidy procurement and still carry serious supply chain risk if a critical reagent has only one qualified source. ### **How is lab equipment procurement different from buying consumables?** Consumables are recurring, relatively low-value, and driven by consumption rates, so they suit thresholds and automated reordering. Equipment is the opposite: infrequent, high-value, and tied to decisions about space, power, ventilation, service contracts, validation, and eventual decommissioning. Equipment purchases also need EHS and facilities input before the order is placed, not after. The two need different processes, and treating capital purchases like consumables is where most equipment procurement goes wrong. ### **How should a new lab phase its instrumentation and equipment procurement?** Start from the science you need to run in your first year, not from a full wish list. Identify the instruments that block work if they're absent, then sequence everything else against build milestones and available budget. Involve facilities and safety early, since ventilation, benching, storage, and waste routes constrain what you can install and where. Anything you can access through a shared facility or core in year one is a purchase you can defer. Our post on [**why lab software ROI starts with implementation**](https://www.scisure.com/blog/lab-software-roi-starts-with-implementation) makes a related point about digital systems: the purchase is the easy part. ### **What is a guided procurement system?** A guided procurement system steers buyers toward approved suppliers, contracted pricing, and preferred products at the point of ordering, rather than relying on people to remember policy. In a lab context it usually means a catalogue that surfaces the negotiated option first, routes anything unusual for approval, and captures the data needed for spend reporting. It works best when it's connected to what the lab already holds in stock, so buyers can see whether a purchase is necessary before they make it. ### **Do we need lab procurement services or a consultant?** It depends on where the gap is. If you lack in-house purchasing capacity, or you're standing up a programme from scratch, external procurement support can be worth it and many labs work this way successfully, particularly smaller organisations without a dedicated function. If the problem is that nobody knows what's already on the shelf, that's an inventory visibility problem, and a consultant will hit the same wall your team does until the underlying data improves. ### **How does inventory management reduce lab supply costs?** Mostly by preventing purchases you didn't need. Accurate stock records stop duplicate orders, expiration tracking flags material that should be used before it's replaced, and consumption data gives you a real basis for deciding whether a bulk discount is a saving or a future disposal fee. Get the right people in the room before the order goes in** Procurement knows sourcing and pricing. Lab operations knows what "right" means for the science. Supply chain management is the wider view, covering where your materials originate, how many suppliers you depend on for a given item, lead times, and what happens if one of them fails. Together, these two processes can help your business save money and improve efficiency. ### What is Sourcing? Therefore, it pays to understand the difference between the various functions — starting with the key differences between sourcing and purchasing. First, sourcing includes finding products or services internally and through partnerships or joint ventures with other companies. On the other hand, purchasing refers to acquiring products or services from outside your company. It could include buying products or services from suppliers, off-the-shelf providers, or even through auctions or online bidding. Second, sourcing usually involves a longer lead time than purchasing. It means that you might have to wait for the product or service to be produced before you can start using it. On the other hand, purchasing can often take less time due to the speed of the supply chain. Third, sourcing is more cost-intensive than purchasing. It is because you will likely have to pay more for the product or service than if you bought it from an external provider. Additionally, you may have to account for any additional costs associated with procuring the product or service, such as transportation and customs fees. Finally, sourcing is about finding quality products from independent producers or small businesses. Purchasing is about buying products from larger, more established companies. ## Procurement vs. Purchasing vs. Sourcing **Procurement** is typically used when acquiring new goods or services. It is the process of searching for the best possible deal from suppliers. The goal is to find the business's lowest price and best quality. It can be done through direct contact with suppliers or through intermediaries such as commercial agents, brokers, or distributors. It can be done through direct purchases from suppliers, intermediaries, formal contracts, or informal arrangements. The goal of purchasing is to obtain lower costs and faster delivery times. Purchasing can also involve issuing written contracts between buyers and sellers. **Sourcing** is when a business finds a supplier who can provide them with the goods or services they need at a reasonable price. Finding a good supplier is not easy because it takes time and effort. The advantage of sourcing is that businesses can ensure they're getting high-quality products at a fair price. Definition, Process, and Examples** Purchasing is the process of acquiring goods or services for a business, identifying a need, selecting a supplier, and completing the transaction, usually by issuing a purchase order. It is the transactional part of buying, and it sits inside the broader function of procurement. The simplest example is a company’s day-to-day buying, like ordering a laptop from CDW or Amazon Business. > **In short: purchasing is the act of buying goods or services a business needs, from raising the request to issuing the purchase order and receiving the goods. Procurement is the wider strategy around it — sourcing suppliers, negotiating contracts, and managing vendor relationships. Purchasing is one step inside procurement, not a synonym for it.** For instance, buying a laptop from CDW or Amazon.com illustrates the purchasing process. The main activity in the [purchasing process](https://www.procuredesk.com/simplifying-your-purchasing-process/?utm_source=glossary&utm_medium=backlink&utm_content=purchasing) is to complete the purchase transaction. A buyer can finalize the transaction by issuing a purchase order to the vendor, placing an order through a website, or simply calling the vendor. Whether an organization issues a purchase order depends on its maturity. A small company might not have a formal purchase order process, while a growing company typically issues purchase orders to vendors. ## **Importance Of Purchasing In Business** Purchasing is crucial for maintaining operational efficiency and managing business spending effectively. It ensures that the right products and services are procured at the right prices, contributing to cost savings and supporting the long-term goals of the organization. A well-defined purchasing process aligns with the overall corporate strategy and supports effective financial management. ## **Key Differences Between Purchasing And Procurement** While often used interchangeably, there is a significant difference between procurement and purchasing. Purchasing is a subset of procurement, focusing specifically on the transaction of buying goods and services. In contrast, procurement encompasses the broader process of identifying needs, sourcing potential suppliers, negotiating contracts, and managing supplier relationships. ### **Differences:** **Purchasing:** Involves the act of acquiring goods and services. **Procurement:** Encompasses the entire process from identifying needs to managing supplier relationships and ensuring compliance with organizational policies. | Aspect | Purchasing | Procurement | | --- | --- | --- | | Scope | Transactional: buy the item | Strategic: source, negotiate, manage suppliers | | Trigger | A specific need (e.g., a laptop) | An ongoing category of spend | | Key output | Purchase order, goods received | Supplier contracts, cost savings, risk control | | Owner | Buyer / purchasing agent | Procurement or finance leadership | | Timeframe | Per transaction | Continuous | ## ## **Examples of purchasing** Purchasing covers any business buy, from routine supplies to large one-off orders. Common examples: * **Office and facility supplies** — reordering printer toner, coffee, or cleaning supplies from Staples or Grainger. * **IT equipment** — buying laptops and monitors from CDW for a new hire. * **Lab or production inputs** — a biotech ordering reagents from Thermo Fisher against a project budget. * **MRO items** — maintenance parts from McMaster-Carr to keep equipment running. * **Services** — engaging a contractor or software subscription through a purchase order. In each case the purchasing process is the same: a need is identified, a request is raised and approved, a purchase order is issued, and the goods or services are received and matched to an invoice. ## **Steps In The Purchasing Process** The purchasing process varies from company to company. A small company might not have a process at all, while a large company might have a highly bureaucratic process. Here are the key steps in the purchasing process: ### **1. Need Identification** The first step is determining what needs to be purchased and why. For example, a new laptop may be needed for a new hire. ### **2. Requesting Quotes** This step involves obtaining quotes from different potential suppliers to assess the best value. Quotes can be obtained formally or informally through vendor websites. ### **3. Purchase Order Approval** The [purchase order approval](https://www.procuredesk.com/purchase-order-process/?utm_source=glossary&utm_medium=backlink&utm_content=purchasing) process ensures that a manager or appropriate person approves the purchase. This step is critical for budget checks and verifying the necessity of the purchase. ### **4. snippet: PaperSave, Webiplex Docupeak, and Paramount Workplace are now part of PairSoft [![PairSoft AP Automation and Document Management Solution](https://www.pairsoft.com/wp-content/themes/wp-pairsoft/assets/images/logo-white.png)](/) [Home](/) / [Resources](/resources/) / [Blog](https://www.pairsoft.com/blog/) # Procurement, Purchasing and Sourcing — What’s the Difference? Janet Martin ![Procurement, Purchasing and Sourcing— What’s the Difference?](https://www.pairsoft.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/shutterstock_1667439013-scaled-e1652165860799-600x261.jpg) ###### Procurement ###### Blog Terms like procurement, purchasing, and sourcing are often used interchangeably. Purchase orders and requisition documents are another set of similarly confused terms. And furthermore, there are even compound versions like purchase requisitions and procurement orders. While the terminology is all related, each has a distinct meaning, and a working understanding of the distinctions helps us gain a better understanding of the overarching procurement cycle. So here we’ll take a closer look at procurement, purchasing and sourcing to answer the question, “What’s the difference?” We’ve also dropped in a quick set of reference statistics about each term to help illustrate its importance to the organization. ## What is Procurement? Procurement is the business function concerned with acquiring (procuring) the goods and services that are vital to an organization. So, procurement is essentially the umbrella term under which you’ll find purchasing, sourcing, requisitions and purchase orders. Procurement involves a [number of steps](https://www.pairsoft.com/procurement-risks-action-items/), with each step in the procurement process presenting both risks and opportunities for efficiency gains. To add another term to the mix, the process of purchasing goods and services is often referred to as the [Procure-to-Pay Cycle](https://www.pairsoft.com/guide-building-a-procure-to-pay-business-case/). The commonly acknowledged major steps in the cycle include: 1. Needs recognition 2. Requesting goods and services 3. Review and approval 4. Sourcing 5. Purchase order 6. Receipt of goods or services 7. Receipt of invoice 8. Pay invoice ## Why is Procurement Important? A well-designed procurement process helps an organization: * [Gain control over and insight into spend.](https://www.pairsoft.com/purchasing-management-software/) * [Minimize errors and fraudulent spending.](https://www.pairsoft.com/keeping-the-records-straight-in-procurement-process/) * [Boost efficiency by streamlining procure-to-pay cycle.](https://www.pairsoft.com/integrating-purchasing-and-payables/) ## What is Purchasing? Purchasing refers to the portion of the procurement cycle that is actively engaged in buying a product or service from a supplier. Think of purchasing as the transactional portion of procurement. If procurement is the subject, then purchasing is the verb. Tasks that directly relate to the process of how goods and services are ordered are purchasing while activities such as strategic sourcing and vendor contract negotiation constitute procurement. ## Why is Purchasing Important? Purchasing is a subset of procurement where the savings can really add up: * Save money by [organizing, consolidating and optimizing purchases](https://www.pairsoft.com/5-ways-to-save-in-the-procurement-process/). * Increase visibility with [requisitions](https://www.pairsoft.com/products-requisition-procurement/mobile-catalog-shopping-approvals/) and [purchase orders](https://www.pairsoft.com/products-requisition-procurement/enterprise-purchase-order-management/) that organize, identify and track purchase requests. * Boost efficiency with tools including guided buying catalogs, [mobile requisitions](https://www.pairsoft.com/products-requisition-procurement/mobile-catalog-shopping-approvals/) and [automated approval routing](https://www.pairsoft.com/products-requisition-procurement/dynamic-rule-engine-approval-workflow/). ## What is Sourcing? As the term implies, sourcing is concerned with finding the best supplier for goods and services. Sourcing is the subset of procurement that comes before any purchases are made. Here we can tack on another term: strategic sourcing. [Strategic sourcing](https://www.pairsoft.com/smart-sourcing/) generally refers to a process of developing supply channels at the greatest value, not just the lowest purchase price. While it might sound simple, it is a broad and far-reaching subject. It’s noteworthy that there are certification programs and even degree programs available to teach the specifics of strategic sourcing. ## Why is Sourcing Important? Sourcing adds value to the procurement cycle: * [Strong supplier relationships](https://www.pairsoft.com/3-powerful-benefits-of-strong-supplier-relationships/) help ensure consistent quality and availability. * [Vendor contracts](https://www.pairsoft.com/products-requisition-procurement/powerful-vendor-contract-management/) and [purchase orders](https://www.pairsoft.com/nine-benefits-of-pos/) spell out terms and eliminate potential misunderstandings. * Businesses with the most advanced collaboration with suppliers [outperform peers by a twofold margin](https://www.mckinsey.com/practice-clients/operations/the-power-of-successful-supplier-collaboration). ## Is it a Purchase Order or a Requisition? These two terms are often used interchangeably, but they serve different purposes and are used in different stages of the procurement cycle. * Requisitions are internal documents. A requisition is a form that an internal department or individual submits listing items it wants to order from an outside vendor. Once these [requests are approved](https://www.pairsoft.com/approvingthespend/), the organization issues purchase orders to suppliers for the requested goods or services. * [Purchase Orders](https://www.pairsoft.com/nine-benefits-of-pos/) are official documents issued to your suppliers, and when accepted form legally binding contracts. Purchase orders detail the items a purchaser agrees to purchase at a certain price point. Among other information, the purchase order also outlines the delivery date, shipping arrangements and payment terms. ## Whatever we call it — it adds value While correct terminology is important, what’s more important is the understanding of the vital role [procurement and its related sub-components](https://www.pairsoft.com/2018-guide-to-creating-synergy-among-procurement-finance-and-accounting/) play in the success of an organization. Research shows that companies with high performing procurement organizations have profit margins [15% higher than the average company](https://www.ibm.com/downloads/cas/9E0QA0DQ?mhq=procurement&mhsrc=ibmsearch_a). Deloitte has found that strategic sourcing and procurement improvements can yield savings of [5-20% across multiple categories](https://www2.deloitte.com/au/en/pages/operations/solutions/sourcing-procurement.html). Becoming a high performing procurement organization first requires an understanding of how the elements of procurement work together and how each contributes to the [overall success](https://www.pairsoft.com/5-proven-ways-to-measure-procurement-performance/) of the procurement function. **Related:** [Glossary of Terminology in Procure-to-Pay Lifecycle](https://www.pairsoft.com/p2p-from-a-to-z-a-glossary-of-terminology-in-the-procure-to-pay-life-cycle/) **Related:** [Integrating Purchasing and Payables](https://www.pairsoft.com/2018-guide-to-creating-synergy-among-procurement-finance-and-accounting/) ## What's stopping your procurement process? We’ll discuss your current challenges and show you how ProcureDesk can streamline processes.* ## What Is Lab Procurement? Lab procurement involves the processes scientists and other research members follow to purchase equipment and supplies for the lab. It typically includes the following steps: * **Needs Identification & Requisition Creation:** Lab staff identify required items and create purchase requisitions with details. * **Review & Approval:** Requisitions are reviewed and approved, considering budget and necessity. * **Vendor Selection & PO Generation:** Vendors are chosen based on criteria like quality and price, and purchase orders (POs) are generated. * **Goods Receipt & Inspection:** Received items are inspected for conformity to specifications and quality. * **Invoice Processing & Payment:** Invoices are verified against POs and receipts before payment is processed. ## Challenges with Lab Procurement These are the three most common challenges we’ve heard in our experience working with life sciences and biotech companies: ### Manual Procurement Processes The manual purchase approval process is often rooted in the traditional organizational structure, where decisions require input and authorization from multiple departments or individuals. As a result, the procurement process can become convoluted and time-consuming. Approvals are often communicated through emails, paper forms, or in-person meetings, leading to potential miscommunication, delays, and administrative overhead. ### Wrong Pricing or Partial Information The lack of a unified and updated system for product catalog management can result in incorrect pricing or partial information. Without a centralized repository for accurate product specifications, vendors may provide inconsistent information or outdated pricing. Moreover, manual data entry and communication can introduce errors, further complicating the procurement process. ### Manual Order Tracking Manual order tracking results from fragmented communication and inadequate visibility into the supply chain. If you’re working with numerous suppliers — each with its own timeline and communication method — tracking the progress of orders becomes a complex task. And if laboratories don’t have a way of tracking **real-time** order statuses, they’re vulnerable to disruptions in research schedules and resource allocation. ## What Is Lab Procurement Software? A lab procurement software **automates the purchasing process for lab equipment and supplies.** It empowers lab personnel to effortlessly manage the entire procurement lifecycle, from requisition to purchase order and receipt of supplies.
